lesson.title: Python Pandas Fundamentals Lab
lesson.goal: load a CSV with pandas, then select, filter, clean and group the data

steps.title: Install pandas and create dataset
steps.instructions: In an empty project folder run `uv init . && uv add pandas` (or `pip install pandas`). Create orders.csv with headers OrderID,CustomerName,Product,Category,Quantity,Price,OrderDate,Shipped,Country and a few sample order rows.

targets.caption: Verify pandas is installed in the project environment

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip vs pip3 or uv virtual environments

hints: Open your integrated terminal inside the empty project folder.
Run pip install pandas (or pip3 install pandas on Mac/Linux, or uv init . followed by uv add pandas).
Create orders.csv in the root of the project folder with the OrderID,CustomerName,Product,Category,Quantity,Price,OrderDate,Shipped,Country header.
common_mistakes: Using pip instead of pip3 on macOS or Linux.
Forgetting to activate the virtual environment or run uv init before uv add pandas.
Placing orders.csv in a different directory than the script.

steps.title: Load CSV data in Python
steps.instructions: Create main.py that imports pandas as pd, loads orders.csv with pd.read_csv into df, and prints df. Run it (python main.py or uv run main.py) to see the rows and table dimensions.

targets.caption: Load orders.csv into a DataFrame named df
Printed table with its rows x columns size

explanations.topic: Aliasing pandas as pd and DataFrame vs Series
CSV structure and automatic row indices

hints: Start main.py by importing pandas with the standard pd alias.
Call pd.read_csv("orders.csv") and assign the result to df.
Add print(df) and execute uv run main.py or python main.py.
common_mistakes: Misspelling the filename or passing a relative path that does not match orders.csv.
Running python main.py outside the virtual environment where pandas was installed.
steps.code: import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"); print(df)

steps.title: Load CSV in Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb, select a Python kernel, and in the first cell import pandas and read orders.csv into df. Run print(df) in a second cell to display the table.

targets.caption: Load the CSV in the first notebook cell

explanations.topic: Why Jupyter notebooks and independent cells help data exploration
Installing the Python extension for Jupyter support

hints: Use the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P) to create a new Jupyter Notebook or create notebook.ipynb directly.
Select your Python interpreter or virtual environment kernel before running the cell.
Put import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") in cell 1, then print(df) in cell 2.
common_mistakes: Selecting a global Python kernel instead of the project virtual environment where pandas is installed.
Running cell 2 before executing cell 1 so df is not yet defined.
steps.code: import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"); print(df)

steps.title: Explore DataFrame structure and stats
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, inspect your DataFrame with df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.columns and df.index. Run each cell to see rows, column types, and summary statistics.

targets.caption: Run exploration methods and attributes to inspect the DataFrame

explanations.topic: Previewing first and last rows with head() and tail()
Viewing non-null counts, dtypes, and descriptive statistics

hints: Note that head(), tail(), info(), and describe() are methods requiring parentheses.
Notice that df.columns and df.index are attributes without parentheses.
Run df.index in a cell to verify the RangeIndex output.
common_mistakes: Adding parentheses to df.columns() or df.index(), which raises a TypeError.
Omitting parentheses on df.info or df.describe and only printing the bound method.
steps.code: df.head(); df.tail(); df.info(); df.describe(); df.columns; df.index

steps.title: Select columns and index rows
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, select multiple columns with double brackets like df[["Country", "Product"]]. Then read one field with integer-location indexing such as df.iloc[10]["Shipped"].

targets.caption: Index rows by integer position with iloc and extract column values

explanations.topic: Single column Series vs multi-column DataFrame indexing

hints: Pass a list of column names inside df[...] so you have double square brackets.
Use df.iloc[10] to fetch the row at integer index 10.
Chain ["Shipped"] onto df.iloc[10] to extract that single cell value.
common_mistakes: Passing two column names with single brackets df["Country", "Product"], which causes a KeyError.
Using parentheses instead of square brackets with iloc, like df.iloc(10).

steps.title: Filter rows with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, filter rows with boolean masks combined by & and |, comparisons like df["Quantity"] > 2, .str.startswith("A"), and ~df["Country"].isin([...]).

targets.caption: Combine boolean masks, string methods, and .isin() filters

explanations.topic: Combining boolean conditions with & and | operators
String filtering with .str and inverting masks with ~

hints: Wrap each condition in parentheses when combining them with & or |.
Access string helpers on a Series with .str, such as df["CustomerName"].str.startswith("A").
Prefix the condition with ~ to negate an .isin([...]) filter.
common_mistakes: Using Python keywords and/or instead of bitwise &/| between pandas Series.
Omitting parentheses around each comparison when using & or |, causing operator precedence errors.

steps.title: Update values and drop rows
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, update rows conditionally with df.loc[condition, column] = value and normalize text with .str.upper(). Remove a row by index with df = df.drop(<index>) and verify with df.tail().

targets.caption: Use .loc[row_condition, column] to update values in place
Drop a row by index, then check df.tail()

explanations.topic: Label-based selection and updating with df.loc
Updating an entire column and dropping rows with df.drop

hints: Pass both a row boolean condition and a target column name inside df.loc[condition, column] = new_value.
Reassign df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper() to convert all country names to uppercase.
Assign the result of df.drop(39) back to df so the row removal persists.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without assigning back to df or passing inplace=True.
Using chained indexing like df[cond]["Product"] = ... instead of df.loc[cond, "Product"] = ...
steps.code: df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna Ivanova", "Product"] = "Tim"; df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"; df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper(); df = df.drop(39)

steps.title: Clean nulls and rename columns
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, handle missing data with df.dropna() and df.fillna({...}, inplace=True). Rename a column in place with df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True).

targets.caption: Clean null values and rename columns with inplace=True

explanations.topic: Dropping or filling missing values and how inplace=True works

hints: Pass a dictionary mapping column names to fill values into df.fillna(...).
Include inplace=True inside fillna or rename to modify df directly without reassignment.
Pass a dictionary {"old_name": "new_name"} to the columns parameter of df.rename().
common_mistakes: Forgetting inplace=True or reassignment on df.rename(...), leaving the column names unchanged.
Assigning df = df.rename(..., inplace=True), which overwrites df with None.
steps.code: df.dropna(); df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True); df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True)

steps.title: Group, sort, and export CSV
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, analyze the data with value_counts(), groupby(...).sum() and sort_values(..., ascending=False). Export the DataFrame with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False).

targets.caption: Aggregate totals per group and export the cleaned CSV

explanations.topic: Counting frequencies with value_counts() and aggregating with groupby()
Sorting rows and exporting without index using to_csv()

hints: Call .groupby("Country")["Price"].sum() to compute total price per country.
Use ascending=False in sort_values() to order from highest to lowest price.
Pass index=False to df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False) so the index column is not written.
common_mistakes: Omitting index=False in to_csv(), which writes an extra unnamed index column to the CSV.
Forgetting to aggregate after groupby(), which only returns a DataFrameGroupBy object.
steps.code: df["Country"].value_counts(); df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum(); df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False); df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False)
